Re: The Antrim Rose

TimPat, the last note of the tune is often the tonic or key note, but not always. This tune is unmistakably in D, both in parts 1 & 2. Sorry to disagree with bogman. Granted, the e is an important note in part 2 but it is there to create tension, not to shift the tonality.

Incidentally, this tune is perfectly adapted to the Scottish pipe. The e’s in the 2nd part harmonise of course very well with the drone in (nominal) A, suggesting perhaps a shift to A.
But the tune is firmy rooted, extatically so, in D ionian.
It totally shreds! What a rocker!
I recommand you listen to Dàimh who recorded it and also brought it to Rathlin, Co. Antrim, during a festival 20 years ago. Pure bliss!

The Antrim Rose, X:5

Transcribed from John William’s virtuoso concertina performance on Solas’ eponymous debut album! I’ve left out left-hand chord notes as well as various grace notes, apart from where the latter have a distinctly rhythmic effect. Note that these (rhythmic) grace notes are, in most instances, not immediately adjacent - as they would typically be on e.g. flute or fiddle - due to the button layout and bellows-direction nature of the Anglo concertina. Also, Solas continue into The Atlantic Wave, in G major, hence the ending on G.

↳ Posted by OMG on April 10th, 2026.
